newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower, bounce fades.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower, bounce fades.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower across the board Wednesday on moderate volumes, after Tuesday's shortcovering bounce ran into more trade selling in gold and silver, traders said.

"Gold opened lower in the U.S. after more trade selling in Europe, then recovered on some shortcovering, but didn't get above yesterdays high, so it's still not a very good performance, especially when you consider some of the buying this week has been funds rolling short positions into the December contract," said Scott Mehlman, chief bullion dealer at Credit Lyonnais Rouse in New York.

COMEX August gold ended down $2.10 at $318.90 an ounce, after recovering from a morning low at $316.20 to a session high at $321.30. The COMEX August/December spread narrowed to $3.60 an ounce Wednesday, from $5.60 six weeks ago.

In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $318.00/50, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $317.30, the London Wednesday morning fix at $315.75, and the New York close Tuesday around $319.80/30.

COMEX August gold looked to be consolidating for now within the $325.80-314.60 range set by Monday's high volume day, while working off its technically oversold condition, analysts said. COMEX gold volume was estimated at 39,000 lots Wednesday, compared to a huge 124,948 lots Monday.

But COMEX gold open interest rose a further 4,545 lots to 217,966 contracts Tuesday, suggesting funds were still putting on short positions on COMEX, while OTC market activity was also rising, as "hedge funds front-run the central banks", as one analyst said.

The CFTC data issued Monday showed funds already had record net short positions of 67,011 contracts on July 1, before the latest slide in gold prices to 12 year lows, which began last Thursday after news the Australian central bank had sold 167 tonnes of gold.
Under pressure from the Australian mining industry, the Australian Prime Minister, John Howard, issued a statement Wednesday defending the move by the Reserve Bank of Australia.

Howard claimed the RBA's move was "a sensible, prudent, completely unexceptional and utterly defensible decision in the interests of Australia and in the interests of us all in deciding to sell gold and put the proceeds into some interest bearing securities."
But the World Gold Council questioned the financial rationale for central bank gold disposals.

"Even the Bank of England has acknowledged that the yield available on lending gold is currently better than what is available in short term Japanese and some German interest rate markets," said George Milling-Stanley, New York-based manager of market analysis for the World Gold Council.
Implied lease rate for gold rose further to over 2.00 percent in most maturities Wednesday.
"It's unfair to put all the blame for the slide in gold prices on central banks, but certainly they haven't helped by failing to clarify their intentions with regard to their reserves," he said.
COMEX September silver ended down 1.5 cents at $4.320 an ounce, but held above the contract low at $4.175 an ounce seen Tuesday.

NYMEX October platinum ended down $5.40 at $381.10 an ounce, and NYMEX September palladium closed down $9.00 at $154.75 an ounce, ahead of the expected resumption of Russian platinum group metal (PGMs) exports this week, following a six month suspension.

"We hear Russian PGM exports have begun arriving in Japan today, but the metal is for consumers and will go in-the-door and out again, so the market will likely stay backwardated and borrowing will continue from the vaults in Zurich, keeping lease rates high, until manufacturers are convinced the situation has stabilized," one refining source said.

One month lease rates for platinum remained offered around 60 percent Wednesday, with one month lease rates for palladium around 80 pct, and palladium sponge was at a premium of $5.00-$10.00 over ingot.
